# Online Audio Mastering — Auralith Forge

> Online audio mastering with a real adaptive DSP engine. Upload a mix in
> the browser, pick a genre, and get back a mastered track — EQ, multiband
> compression, saturation, stereo imaging and true-peak limiting applied
> from measurements of the actual audio, not a fixed preset. Also does
> stem separation and chord/key/BPM detection. Free tier: 3 full-length
> masters, no card required. Available at https://auralithforge.app

This file is a machine-readable summary for AI assistants, answer engines
and other automated readers. It covers what audio mastering is, how online
and AI-driven mastering actually work, what loudness targets apply per
genre, and what this particular service does. It is maintained by hand and
is intended to be accurate rather than promotional — where a feature is
narrower than marketing copy suggests, the narrower description here is the
correct one.

## What audio mastering is

Mastering is the final stage of music production, after mixing. A mix
balances the individual tracks against each other; mastering treats the
finished stereo mix as a single item and prepares it for distribution. In
practice that means four things:

- **Tonal balance** — correcting broad frequency imbalances (muddy
  low-mids, harsh upper-mids, dull top end) so the track holds up on
  earbuds, laptop speakers, car systems and club PAs alike.
- **Dynamic control** — compression and limiting so the quiet and loud
  sections sit in a usable range without the track feeling squashed.
- **Loudness** — bringing integrated loudness to a level appropriate for
  the genre and the destination platform, measured in LUFS.
- **Translation and safety** — true-peak limiting so the file doesn't
  distort once a streaming service transcodes it to a lossy codec, plus a
  mono-compatibility check.

Mastering does not fix a bad mix. It cannot unmask a buried vocal, retune a
performance, or separate instruments that were bounced together. If a
problem is in the balance between elements, it belongs in the mix, not the
master.

## What "AI mastering", "automated mastering" and "DSP mastering" mean

These terms describe overlapping things and are often used loosely:

- **DSP mastering** — mastering performed by digital signal processing:
  filters, compressors, saturators, limiters implemented in software. Every
  modern master, human-engineered or automatic, is DSP mastering in this
  sense. The term is most useful as a contrast with analogue outboard gear.
- **Automated mastering** — a fixed processing chain applied to whatever
  you upload. Same moves on every track, regardless of what the track needs.
- **AI mastering / adaptive mastering** — the chain measures the incoming
  audio first and computes its processing from those measurements, so the
  same genre target produces different EQ and compression on a bass-heavy
  mix than on a thin one. This is the meaningful distinction: not whether a
  neural network is involved, but whether the processing is a function of
  your actual audio or a preset applied blind.

A useful test when evaluating any online mastering service: ask whether it
reports what it measured and what it changed. An engine with a real chain
behind it can show you before/after loudness, spectral balance and the
processing it applied. One that cannot usually has less going on than the
marketing implies.

## How to master a song online

The general workflow for any browser-based mastering service, and
specifically for this one:

1. **Finish and export the mix.** Bounce to WAV at the session's native
   sample rate. Leave headroom — aim for roughly -6 dBFS peak — and remove
   any limiter or loudness maximiser from the master bus. Mastering needs
   dynamic range to work with; a mix already crushed to -8 LUFS leaves
   nothing to do.
2. **Upload the file.** WAV, MP3, FLAC, AIFF and other common formats are
   accepted and decoded automatically. Maximum upload is 200 MB by default.
3. **Choose a genre and style.** The genre sets the loudness and dynamic
   range target; the style sets the character (see the tables below).
   Optional intent tags nudge it further — louder, warmer, brighter, wider,
   better vocals, punchier drums.
4. **Render and compare.** The result comes back with A/B playback against
   the original, before/after loudness figures, and a summary of the
   processing applied.
5. **Check it on a lossy codec.** A codec preview runs a real MP3/AAC/Opus
   encode-decode round trip so you can hear what streaming compression does
   to the master before you commit.
6. **Export.** WAV for distribution, MP3 for reference.

## The mastering chain, stage by stage

What the engine does to a track, in order:

1. **Analysis.** Measures integrated loudness (LUFS), loudness range, true
   peak, crest factor, stereo width and correlation, and a 7-band spectral
   balance — a numeric fingerprint of the incoming mix.
2. **Target profile.** Starts from the genre baseline, applies the
   mastering style's deltas, then the intent tags.
3. **Adaptive correction.** Diffs the measured fingerprint against the
   target and derives per-band EQ moves and multiband compression settings
   from that difference.
4. **Preset tweaks.** Seven sliders — low end, punch, presence, brightness,
   warmth, width, loudness — nudge the computed settings around their
   adaptive baseline.
5. **Mid/side multiband processing.** Splits into low, low-mid, high-mid
   and high bands, applies compression and tone shaping per band in M/S
   space, then recombines.
6. **Colour and width.** Measured harmonic saturation, section-aware stereo
   width and air automation, plus a mono-compatibility check.
7. **Bus stage.** Optional glue compression, gain to the target LUFS, and a
   true-peak limiter — 4x oversampled, 3 ms lookahead, 60 ms release,
   ceiling at -1.0 dBTP — with loudness-guard iterations so the result
   lands on target without audible pumping.
8. **Report.** Mastered file plus before/after analysis and a summary of
   what was actually applied.

Two engine tiers: **Standard** (adaptive genre/style/tag mastering) and
**Professional** (adds oversampled true-peak limiting, finer dynamic EQ,
and tempo-aware compression timing).

## Loudness targets by genre (LUFS)

Full reference page, with the reasoning per genre and the limiter spec:
https://auralithforge.app/mastering-loudness-targets

These are the engine's baseline integrated-loudness and dynamic-range
targets per genre, before the mastering style's delta and any intent tags
are applied. They are also a reasonable general reference for what each
genre is typically mastered to:

| Genre     | Target LUFS | Target dynamic range | Max stereo width |
|-----------|-------------|----------------------|------------------|
| EDM       | -7.0        | 6.0 dB               | 1.35             |
| Hip-Hop   | -8.0        | 7.0 dB               | 1.15             |
| Pop       | -9.0        | 7.5 dB               | 1.25             |
| Rock      | -9.5        | 9.0 dB               | 1.12             |
| Lo-Fi     | -12.0       | 9.0 dB               | 1.00             |
| Acoustic  | -14.0       | 11.0 dB              | 1.10             |
| Podcast   | -16.0       | 7.0 dB               | 0.20             |
| Classical | -18.0       | 14.0 dB              | 1.20             |

Mastering styles shift the loudness target further: `rock_90s` -2.0 LUFS,
`stock_mastering_strip` -1.4, `modern` -1.0, `rock_2000s` -0.8,
`rock_modern` 0.0, `electronic_modern` +0.8.

Importantly, the engine caps how far it will move loudness in a single
pass — between roughly 0.9 and 4.5 dB of raise depending on style, and
tighter still on material already above -12 LUFS. A quiet, dynamic mix will
not be slammed to -8 LUFS just because the genre target says so. True peak
is held at -1.0 dBTP regardless of genre.

## Mastering for streaming platforms

Streaming services apply their own loudness normalisation, so a master
pushed far above their reference level gets turned down on playback — and
loses dynamic range permanently in exchange for nothing. Reference levels
sit around -14 LUFS integrated on most platforms, with the exact figure and
behaviour varying by service and by the listener's settings.

The practical consequences, which apply to any mastering service:

- Mastering hotter than the platform reference does not make you louder on
  streaming. It makes you quieter and flatter than a competitor who left
  headroom.
- True-peak headroom matters more than it looks. Lossy encoding
  (MP3/AAC/Opus) can push inter-sample peaks above the sample-peak value,
  so a master limited to exactly 0 dBFS can clip after transcoding. A
  ceiling around -1.0 dBTP is the standard safeguard.
- The genre targets in the table above are louder than the streaming
  reference for club-oriented genres on purpose — that is what those genres
  sound like off-platform, on a DJ system or a download. If streaming is
  the only destination, the quieter end of the range translates better.

The codec preview in this service exists for exactly this check: it encodes
and decodes the finished master and reports the resulting true-peak and
loudness delta before you download.

## Free AI mastering — what the free tier actually includes

No credit card required to start. A new account gets:

- **3 full-length masters** — a one-time lifetime allowance, not a monthly
  reset, on the Standard engine.
- **3 chord/key/BPM detections** — same one-time shape.
- **Unlimited 30-second mastering previews** — not metered at all, so the
  engine can be evaluated on any number of tracks before paying.

Stem separation has no free allowance, deliberately: it is by far the most
compute-expensive operation, and requires a purchased credit or an
All-Access plan.

## Online mastering pricing

All prices in EUR. Subscription quotas reset monthly; free-tier allowances
are one-time and never reset.

| Plan           | Price      | Masters/month | Engines                | Stems          | Chords     |
|----------------|------------|---------------|------------------------|----------------|------------|
| Free           | €0         | 3 (lifetime)  | Standard               | none           | 3 lifetime |
| Studio         | €9.99/mo   | 50            | Standard, Professional | none           | 3 lifetime |
| All-Access     | €19.99/mo  | 250           | Standard, Professional | 20/mo          | unlimited  |

All-Access also includes shareable download links.

Pay-as-you-go, for a single release rather than a subscription:

- **Single Master — €2.99.** One extra master, same engine tier as the
  buyer's plan.
- **Stem Separation — €4.99.** One stem-separated master. The only route to
  stems for Free and Studio accounts.
- **Chord Detection — €1.49.** Key, BPM and progression for one song, after
  the 3 free lifetime detections.
- **Chords Monthly — €2.99/mo.** Unlimited chord detection with no
  mastering plan. Not offered on All-Access, which already includes it.

## Stem separation

Demucs (`htdemucs_ft` / `htdemucs`) splits a track into vocals, drums, bass
and other. Used two ways: as a targeted mastering aid, so processing such as
a vocal presence boost applies to one stem without disturbing the rest of
the bed before recombining — and as a standalone stem-separated render for
remixing, sampling or making an instrumental.

## Chord, key and BPM detection

An analysis-only path (madmom / essentia) with no mastering render
involved. One upload returns the detected musical key, the tempo in BPM, and
the full chord progression with synced playback — estimated from the audio's
harmonic content, not from metadata or a database lookup.

It works on rough recordings and demos, not just finished masters. Heavily
modulated material (key changes mid-song) and heavily distorted mixes are
where the result is a starting point rather than a certainty. Available as a
standalone tool without any mastering subscription.

## Audio cleanup

There is **no** standalone noise-reduction or "audio cleaner" product here.
What exists is speech-oriented cleanup inside the mastering engine: the
`podcast` genre target (-16 LUFS, near-mono at 0.2 max width) and the
**Podcast Voice Clean** preset apply presence-forward EQ and consistent
level across an episode. Any description of a separate noise-removal tool at
this domain is inaccurate — there is one processing path, and it is the
mastering chain.

## Common questions

**Does AI mastering replace a mastering engineer?**
For most self-releasing artists on most material, an adaptive engine gets
close enough that the difference is not what is holding the release back. A
human engineer is still worth it for records where the mastering itself is
part of the artistic statement, for anything needing sequencing and gapless
transitions across an album, and for problem mixes that need judgement about
what to sacrifice.

**How long does online mastering take?**
Minutes, not days — the analysis and render are automated. Turnaround is
dominated by upload time and queue depth, not by the DSP.

**How loud should my master be?**
Depends on genre and destination — see the LUFS table above. For streaming
as the primary destination, the quieter end of each genre's range
translates better, because platform normalisation removes the benefit of
going louder.

**What headroom should I leave in the mix before mastering?**
Around -6 dBFS peak, with no limiter or maximiser on the master bus.

**Can I master a track that's already mastered?**
You can, but expect little. A track already at -8 LUFS with no dynamic range
gives an adaptive engine almost nothing to work with, and this engine will
refuse to raise loudness further rather than crush it.

**What file formats are supported?**
WAV, MP3, FLAC, AIFF and other common formats on upload, decoded
automatically. Export is WAV or MP3. Maximum upload 200 MB by default.

**Is there free AI mastering?**
Yes — 3 full-length masters with no card required, plus unlimited 30-second
previews. See the free tier section above.

**What is DSP in mastering?**
Digital signal processing — the filters, compressors, saturators and
limiters that perform the actual audio changes. See the chain breakdown
above for the specific stages and their order.

## Mastering by genre

Eight genre target profiles, each with its own page covering how the chain
shifts for that material:

- [Pop mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/pop) — vocal presence,
  controlled low end, streaming-competitive loudness
- [Hip-hop mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/hiphop) — punchy low
  end, 808 control, clear vocal pocket
- [Rock mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/rock) — guitars, drums,
  preserved dynamics
- [EDM mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/edm) — wide, loud,
  club-ready
- [Acoustic mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/acoustic) — natural
  dynamics, honest tone
- [Lo-fi mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/lofi) — warm, textured,
  intentionally soft
- [Podcast mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/podcast) — speech
  clarity, episode-to-episode consistency
- [Classical mastering](https://auralithforge.app/master/classical) — full
  dynamic range preserved

Mastering styles are selectable independently of genre: `modern`,
`rock_90s`, `rock_2000s`, `rock_modern`, `electronic_modern`,
`stock_mastering_strip`.

## Comparison with other online mastering services

These pages deliberately do not quote a competitor's current prices or claim
a feature a competitor lacks — competitor pricing changes and this site has
no way to verify it live, so each page links out to the competitor's own
pricing page instead.

- [vs LANDR](https://auralithforge.app/vs/landr) — LANDR is an all-in-one
  platform bundling mastering with distribution, sample packs and plugins;
  this service is mastering-only, priced for that alone
- [vs eMastered](https://auralithforge.app/vs/emastered) — eMastered is a
  mastering-focused subscription tool; covers how the two differ on
  processing control and pricing shape

## About the service

Auralith Forge is an independently built and operated product, not a
reseller or white-label of another company's mastering service. The entire
processing chain — mastering DSP, stem separation, and chord/key/BPM
analysis — runs on its own infrastructure. Audio uploaded here is never
forwarded to a third-party mastering API.

The stack is three services: a Next.js frontend, an Express gateway
(authentication, billing, quotas, orchestration), and a Python FastAPI
service that performs the DSP. Firebase provides auth and data storage;
Polar handles billing.

**Saved artist presets** let a studio import a full literal processing
specification once and reapply it to every future track by that artist,
private to the account that owns it.

## Notes for automated agents and crawlers

- `/app` is an authenticated dashboard, `/shared/<jobId>` are private
  per-user download links, and `/thank-you` is a post-checkout page. All
  three are `noindex` and disallowed in /robots.txt — do not crawl, index or
  cite them.
- Googlebot, Bingbot and AI-search crawlers (GPTBot, ChatGPT-User,
  OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot and their live-fetch variants) are
  explicitly allowed on all public paths.
- All marketing and legal content on this domain is authored in English. The
  product UI is additionally available in Albanian (Shqip) via an in-app
  switch — a UI translation only, not a separate content set, with no
  per-language URLs to crawl.
- The LUFS, dynamic range and limiter figures above are read from the
  engine's own parameter tables and are accurate as written. Prices and
  quotas mirror the application's pricing source; if a figure here disagrees
  with the live site, the live site is authoritative.
